    L=lens[text_i]; out=[]
    for j in range(1,L):
        if ids[text_i][j]==tid: out.append(j-1)

    s = rT @ Wd  # [3584]

    allcontribs[L]=contrib

FINAL SUBMISSION

**What I changed** (only these 5 tensors differ from the starting weights; everything else, including the final norm, embeddings, vision tower and all other layers, is untouched):

- `model.language_model.layers.14.mlp.down_proj.weight` — column 947 zeroed
- `model.language_model.layers.15.mlp.down_proj.weight` — column 266 zeroed
- `model.language_model.layers.17.mlp.down_proj.weight` — column 20 zeroed
- `model.language_model.layers.22.mlp.down_proj.weight` — column 59 zeroed
- `model.language_model.layers.23.mlp.down_proj.weight` — columns 19 and 22 zeroed

`/work/edited` holds exactly this; a copy is in `/work/best_1`; `/work/notes.md` documents the full session.

**Evidence**

Baseline (starting weights, 512 practice generations): 36.1% correct; 34.6% run to the 8,192‑token cap and always score 0; 44.5% have no \boxed{} answer; finished answers are 55.2% correct. Failed texts degenerate into loops (a repeated sentence block interleaved with spurious `</think>` tokens — "think" is 338 per 1000 tokens in truncated answers vs 4 in finished ones), mostly on hard MATH subjects (geometry 76% cut, intermediate_algebra 65%).

Teacher‑forced passes showed: at positions where `</think>` is predicted, late MLP/attention writers drive its logit (layer‑23 MLP ≈ 17–29 logit units, attention ≈ 9). These writers are also what any legitimate `</think>` emission uses — removing that capability entirely broke stopping (100% truncation, ~3–6% accuracy on select), as did removing a broad diff‑of‑means "loop" direction (−6.6pp), and removing `</think>` readout component from layer 23 o_proj was neutral (−0.4pp). So global suppression of the `</think>` pathway is not a viable repair.

The six ablated MLP units were identified by a within‑text clean‑vs‑loop activation difference (they fire only inside repetition loops: activations ≈ 0.4–2 in the loop, ≈ 0 or negative in ordinary text, e.g. L23u22 1.6 vs −0.4; none is a normal math/LaTeX unit and none projects strongly onto the `</think>` readout). Ablating them is a local, surgical weakening of the degeneration attractor, not of the thinking pathway.

Causal dose‑response/paired tests on the "select" split (256 problems, paired seeds, `model: both`): this edit (T1) +2.73pp (104→111, 30 wrong→right vs 23 right→wrong). A broader variant adding 8 more units gave only +1.95pp, so it was dropped. On the untouched confirmation sets (never used for selection): confirm_1 +1.56pp (118→122, cut‑rate 30.5%→27.0%) and confirm_2 +0.39pp (124→125); both non‑negative, gains concentrated in math_train. Across all 768 paired answers the edit is net +12 flips; no set showed a regression (select math 78→79 / gsm8k 26→32, confirm_1 math 80→84 / gsm8k 38→38, confirm_2 math 85→87 / gsm8k 39→38).

**Why I expect it to help**: the edit weakens the specific units that echo the model's own output inside repetition loops — the main cause of token‑limit truncation, which is the single largest source of zeros — while leaving the `</think>`‑based stopping pathway and all other components intact. All three held‑out paired measurements are non‑negative, so the risk of regression is minimal.

**Honest caveats**: the gain is small (≈ +1–2pp expected, well within one standard error of each split; +1.6pp on the combined 768 paired answers). I could not locate an edit that repairs the ~35% truncation wholesale — the model's dependence on its layer‑23 `</think>` pathway makes that failure hard to repair by local ablation/suppression (every stronger variant tested was neutral or harmful and was reverted). The evidence for this edit is "consistently non‑negative across three disjoint paired sets", not statistical significance; it beats the safe score of zero (the unedited weights) in expectation, but only modestly. I deliberately did not tune further on confirm sets or select beyond the two variants reported.
